rows: Ancient Door, Magdalen College, Oxford
Talbot photographed an old carved door at Magdalen College in Oxford. Old wood and stone made good early subjects because they showed off the rich detail of his paper negatives.
What do the carvings and nails on the door tell you about its age?
Robert Cornelius, Self-Portrait

In 1839 Robert Cornelius, a Philadelphia chemist, stepped in front of his camera outside his family's shop and held still for a minute or more. It is often called the first photographic portrait of a person, and the first selfie.
What would you do for a whole minute without moving?
The Gardener
Hippolyte Bayard photographed a gardener with his tools around 1840. Bayard liked to show working people, and the picture feels as warm as a small painting.
What tools can you spot?
The Old Bridge of the Change, Lyon
Félix Richard made a daguerreotype of the Pont du Change in Lyon, France, around 1840. It is one of the earliest views of the city and shows a bridge that no longer exists.
What do you think it was like to cross a bridge with houses on it?
View from the Weather Tower, Graz
Carl Rospini photographed the old town of Graz, Austria, on 2 October 1840 from a tower. It is among the oldest photographs of the city, and the roofs and church towers look as if time stopped.
Can you find a church tower among the roofs?
Grandma Toppan
Robert Cornelius made this daguerreotype of an older woman around 1841. Sitters sat in bright sunlight with their eyes shut or squinting to get through the long exposure.
Why do you think the sitter might squint?
The Tuileries Palace, Central Pavilion
Joseph-Philibert Girault de Prangey took this daguerreotype of a palace in Paris in 1841. The Tuileries burned down in 1871, so photographs like this are the only way we can see it.
Why might a photograph of a lost building be precious?
Tree, Path and Cliff
Girault de Prangey photographed a tree beside a path and a cliff, using a daguerreotype plate as shiny as a mirror. Landscapes were harder than buildings, because leaves move in the wind.
How did the wind affect the tree?
Notre-Dame Cathedral, Paris
Girault de Prangey photographed Notre-Dame's front in 1841 on a silver-coated copper plate. It is one of the earliest pictures of the cathedral, taken before it was restored.
What differences do you think there are from today's Notre-Dame?
Horse Dealer's Sign
Bayard photographed the sign of a horse dealer in Paris in 1842. Shop signs were important in a time when many people could not read.
Why would a shop use a picture for its sign?
Bayard in Front of His House
Hippolyte Bayard posed outside his own home in 1842. Bayard invented a photo process the same year as Daguerre but was less famous, so he often photographed himself.
Do you think he looks proud or sad?
The Pantheon, Paris
Alphonse Poitevin photographed a group of visitors on the steps of the Paris Pantheon in 1842. The people stand frozen in time, and they show how a normal crowd dressed that year.
How many people can you spot on the steps?
Lotus Columns at Gournah
Girault de Prangey photographed Egyptian columns at Gournah on a trip through the Middle East in the early 1840s. His daguerreotypes are among the oldest of these ancient places.
What shape are the tops of the columns?
The Old Stock Exchange, Lille
Louis Désiré Blanquart-Evrard photographed the old exchange in Lille, France, in 1842. He later set up a printing workshop that made hundreds of photographic prints for books.
What was a stock exchange used for?
The Cabildo, Buenos Aires
Giovanni Andrea Bianchi made the first daguerreotype of the Cabildo, the old town hall of Buenos Aires, in 1842. It is the oldest photograph of the city's main square.
What buildings stand around a town square where you live?
Tower of Orléans Cathedral
Talbot photographed one of the towers of Orléans Cathedral in France in 1843. He traveled across France to photograph and published the best ones in The Pencil of Nature.
What does the tower have at the top?
View of the Boulevards, Paris
Talbot photographed a wide Paris boulevard from a window in 1843. Photographs from windows were common because they gave a high, safe place for the camera.
What can you see from a window like this?
Sir Walter Scott's Monument, Edinburgh
Talbot photographed the Scott Monument in Edinburgh, still new in 1844. It honors the writer Sir Walter Scott, and Talbot caught it as scaffolding was probably still nearby.
Why do people build monuments to writers?
The Pencil of Nature
This is the cover of The Pencil of Nature, the first book to be illustrated with photographs. Talbot published it in London in parts, from 1844 to 1846, and pasted real photographs onto the pages.
Why was a book of photographs such a big idea?
A-Ma Temple, Macao
Jules Itier, a French customs official, photographed the A-Ma Temple in Macao in 1844. It is one of the oldest photographs made in China.
Why would an official take a camera on a trip to China?
Joseph Vance
Joseph Vance was a congressman from Ohio who sat for Mathew Brady in the 1840s. Brady photographed hundreds of politicians and hung their portraits in his gallery.
What does a politician want you to think about them in a picture?
John Peter Van Ness
John Peter Van Ness was a congressman, banker and mayor of Washington. Brady photographed him in the 1840s as part of his gallery of famous Americans.
What do you think Van Ness is thinking?
York Minster, from Lop Lane
Talbot photographed the great cathedral of York in 1844. A cathedral was a good subject for a camera that needed a long time to expose, because it would not move.
How tall do you think the cathedral is?
John Parker Hale
John P. Hale was a senator from New Hampshire who spoke out against slavery. Brady's gallery made faces like his familiar to Americans.
Why might people want to see the faces of leaders?
The Open Door (Version)
Talbot photographed a door held open with a broom at his home. He later printed it again and used it to show that photography could capture quiet, everyday scenes.
What do you see inside the open door?
St. Lucia, Naples
Calvert Richard Jones, who was a clergyman, photographed the harbor of Santa Lucia in Naples, Italy, in 1846. He used paper negatives, which gave the picture soft light.
What might a harbor have looked like 180 years ago?
The Celebrated Obelisk, Naples
Calvert Jones photographed a tall monument in Naples in 1846. His soft paper pictures were a bit like drawings made of light.
What does an obelisk look like?
The Trellis
Hippolyte Bayard photographed a trellis, a wooden frame that holds up climbing plants, in 1847. It is a very early picture of a garden structure with light and shadow.
What would grow on a trellis?
The Chess Players
Talbot photographed people playing chess around 1847. Staged scenes like this show that he saw the camera as a tool to tell small stories.
Who do you think is winning?
The Artist's Son, Barrett Browning
Robert Browning, the poet, made a picture of his young son, Pen. His wife was the poet Elizabeth Barrett Browning, and their son was a favorite subject.
What would you say to a poet's son?
Pyramid of Khafre, Egypt
Maxime Du Camp photographed the pyramid of Khafre at Giza in 1849. His pictures of Egypt helped start the fashion for photographing faraway places.
How big do you think the pyramid is?
Karnak, Gateway of the Temple of Khonsu
Du Camp photographed a huge gateway at Karnak in Egypt, one of the biggest temple complexes in the world. His pictures were published in an album that became famous.
What do the figures carved on the gateway show?
Temple of Hermonthis
Du Camp photographed a temple in Egypt in 1849, when many ancient buildings were still half buried. The picture was printed in an album of his Egypt trip.
Why were so many temples half buried?
John C. Calhoun
John C. Calhoun was a powerful senator from South Carolina who strongly defended slavery. Mathew Brady photographed him in March 1849, a year before he died.
What do you notice about his face and eyes?
Edgar Allan Poe
This daguerreotype of Edgar Allan Poe was made in June 1849, a few months before he died. It is known as the Annie daguerreotype, because Poe gave it to his friend Annie Richmond.
What do you think he is thinking about?
Puerta del Perdón, Seville Cathedral
Charles Clifford photographed the Gate of Forgiveness at Seville Cathedral in Spain in about 1850. He was a Welsh photographer who worked in Spain for Queen Isabella II.
What patterns do you see on the arch?
Sunset, Horseshoe Fall, Niagara
George Barker photographed Niagara Falls in 1850 and sold the pictures as stereographs to tourists. The water looks like cotton because it moved during the exposure.
Why does the falling water look soft?
John Bidwell
John Bidwell was a California pioneer who later ran for president. This portrait was made from a daguerreotype Brady took of him around 1850.
What do you think a pioneer looks like?
James Fenimore Cooper
James Fenimore Cooper wrote The Last of the Mohicans. This daguerreotype of the author was made by Mathew Brady around 1850.
Have you read a book by this author?
The Barley Mow Inn, Clifton Hampden
Francis Frith photographed an old English pub with a thatched roof. Before he went to Egypt, Frith made a business of selling pictures of towns and villages.
What would you like to eat at an old inn?
Colmore Row, Birmingham
Francis Frith photographed a street in Birmingham, England, where tall buildings and horse carts mix. It is a good example of how street photos show city life of the time.
What would you notice about the traffic?
The Great Pyramid, Giza
This early photograph shows the Great Pyramid and the remains of a causeway leading to it. The pyramid was built about 4,500 years ago for Pharaoh Khufu.
How do you think people moved the stones?
Conwy Castle
Francis Frith photographed Conwy Castle in Wales, a big stone fortress built in the 1280s. His pictures of castles sold well to Victorian tourists.
How many towers can you count?
Woman, Nineteenth-Century Tintype
A tintype is a photograph made on a thin sheet of dark metal. It was cheap and quick to make, so ordinary people could afford portraits.
What does her clothing tell you about her time?
Salon of Baron Gros
Baron Gros was a diplomat who photographed his own sitting room with a daguerreotype around 1850. Crowded with paintings and furniture, it shows how rich people decorated.
How many paintings can you count?
Man, Nineteenth-Century Tintype
A tintype portrait of a man, printed on dark metal. These small pictures were sold at fairs and in towns for a small price.
What do you think the man did for a living?
Neill's Tomb, Lucknow
Francis Frith's series included photographs of the cemetery in Lucknow, India. This tomb is for Brigadier-General James Neill, who died in the 1857 uprising.
Why might people visit a cemetery from a faraway war?
Two Couples, Nineteenth-Century Tintype
Two couples pose together for a tintype in the late 1800s. A tintype could be made in minutes, so friends could take one home the same day.
Why would two couples want a picture together?
The Bridge of Palalda

In 1851 Gustave Le Gray and his friend Auguste Mestral traveled through southern France taking pictures for the government. This picture of an old bridge in Palalda shows the shapes of arches and shadows.
How would you cross the bridge?
An Effect of the Sun, Normandy
Le Gray photographed sunlight breaking through clouds over the sea. He was one of the first to catch dramatic skies, and to do it he joined two negatives together.
How does the light make the water look?
The Large Speos at Abu Simbel
Félix Teynard was a civil engineer who photographed Egypt in 1851 and 1852. His photograph of the Great Temple at Abu Simbel shows the huge statues covered by sand.
Why do you think the statues are partly buried?
Sphinxes at Karnak
Teynard photographed the avenue of sphinxes at Karnak in Egypt, where statues with ram heads line the path. His pictures were known for their careful, calm look.
What animal's head do the sphinxes have?
The Royal Porcelain Factory at Sèvres
Henri-Victor Regnault, a chemist, photographed the royal porcelain factory at Sèvres in France. He was a scientist who used photography to study how light and chemicals worked.
Why would a chemist be interested in photography?
A Bride and Her Bridesmaids
Southworth and Hawes, who ran a studio in Boston, made this large daguerreotype of a bride and her bridesmaids in 1851. Wedding pictures this early are rare.
What do you notice about their dresses?
Landscape with Seated Figure
Frank Chauvassaignes made a mysterious landscape with a person resting by a stream. The sunlight and deep shadows make it look like a painting.
What is the person doing by the stream?
Monuments Carved into Bedrock
Félix Teynard photographed temples cut straight into the rock in Egypt in 1851. He worked in heat and sand, and his pictures were published in a large album.
How do you carve a whole temple out of a cliff?
Studying Laughter
Guillaume Duchenne photographed a man making a laughing face using electricity on his muscles. It was part of the first scientific study of how faces show feelings.
Which muscles do you use to laugh?
Château de Chenonceau
Gustave Le Gray photographed the east side of this castle, built across a river in France, in 1851. It is one of the oldest pictures of a famous castle.
What is unusual about where this castle is built?
Scolopendrium vulgare
Anna Atkins made this picture of a fern by laying a leaf on light-sensitive paper and letting the sun print it blue. In 1843 she made the first book illustrated with photographs.
Can you spot the tiny parts of the fern's leaf?
Amiens Cathedral, Transept
Henri Le Secq photographed the northern side of Amiens Cathedral. Le Secq was a painter's son who photographed Gothic churches with extra care.
How many levels of windows can you count?
Senator George Ellis Pugh
George Pugh was a senator from Ohio. Photographers displayed pictures of politicians in their windows as advertising.
Why would a photographer put pictures of famous people in their window?
Henriette Robert
Louis-Rémy Robert photographed his daughter Henriette seated and looking at the camera. Parents were some of the best photographers of their children.
What do you think she was doing when it was taken?
Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres
Ingres was one of the most admired painters in France. He sat for this photograph in 1852, even though he thought painting was more serious than photography.
Why would a painter let himself be photographed?
Young Man in an Athletic Outfit
Oliver Willard photographed a young man in clothes for sports. People then played sports in clothes that looked like street clothes.
How is his outfit different from what an athlete wears today?
Fountain of Diana, Louvre
Charles Marville and Louis Désiré Blanquart-Évrard photographed a statue of Diana in the Louvre in 1852. The goddess stands with her deer, carved by famous sculptors.
What is the goddess holding?
Trees by the Chailly Road, Fontainebleau
Gustave Le Gray photographed a forest road in Fontainebleau, where painters and photographers liked to work. The dark trees and bright road feel like a painting.
Where does the road lead?
Scotch Firs, Hawkhurst
Benjamin Brecknell Turner photographed tall pine trees in the English countryside. At a time of factories and trains, he chose quiet scenes of trees and old cottages.
What do the tall trees feel like?
Artist with a Pipe
Frank Chauvassaignes photographed an artist, or maybe an assistant, smoking a pipe. The deep light and shadows make this portrait look like a painting from long ago.
What do you think he is thinking about?
Statue of the Virgin, Notre-Dame
Auguste Mestral photographed a statue made for Notre-Dame in Paris around 1853. A sculptor had asked him to photograph his work.
How might a photographer help a sculptor?
Tomb of the Virgin, Jerusalem
Auguste Salzmann photographed the Tomb of the Virgin in Jerusalem in 1854. The French government sent him to take pictures of old buildings in the Holy Land.
Why would a government send a photographer?
Mr. Leroux as Alceste
Julien Vallou de Villeneuve photographed Leroux, an actor from the Comédie-Française, in a role from Molière's play The Misanthrope. The actors posed for photographs like this to promote their shows.
How would an actor pose to look like a character?
Plaster Cast from the Depaulis Collection
Henri Le Secq photographed a plaster copy of a sculpture. Photographing plaster casts was good practice and also helped art students who could not travel.
Why would art students want pictures of sculptures?
House in Pau
An amateur photographer, known only as W.H.G., made this large and richly toned print of a house in Pau, France. Pau was a popular winter resort for British visitors.
What would it be like to live in a house like this?
Eclipse of the Sun
William and Frederick Langenheim of Philadelphia photographed the Sun during the eclipse on May 26, 1854. It is one of the earliest photographs of an eclipse.
Why is it hard to photograph an eclipse?
Nadar, Self-Portrait
Nadar was a French photographer, balloonist and caricaturist who photographed the famous people of Paris. He made self-portraits with a wild mane of red hair and a bold look.
What does his face show about his personality?
The Railway Yard, Balaklava
Roger Fenton photographed the railway yard at Balaklava during the Crimean War. A railway was built in weeks to carry supplies to the soldiers, and Fenton recorded the work.
What do railway workers carry in a war?
The Old Post Office, Balaklava
Fenton photographed a post office in Balaklava. Letters from home were very important to soldiers, and this humble building was the place where they came.
Why would letters matter so much to soldiers?
Landing Place, Railway Stores, Balaklava
Fenton photographed the place where ships unloaded railway supplies. His pictures show war as a big logistics job, with piles of crates and cranes.
What do you see being unloaded?
Landing Place, Ordnance Wharf
This view shows the Ordnance Wharf at Balaklava, where guns and ammunition were landed. Fenton had to work quickly in the heat.
What do you think the soldiers carried?
Encampment of Horse Artillery
Fenton photographed the tents and horses of the Horse Artillery camp. A wagon served as his darkroom, and the heat often ruined his chemicals.
Why would heat ruin photo chemicals?
